studies.title: Counting It Over Again
studies.meaning: Two words open the surah, both intensive forms, and they name a person by a habit rather than by a deed. Classical readers separate them, most taking the first as harm done by gesture and the second by speech, though the sources record the reverse and also treat them as a pair. Then the surah moves to money: gathered and counted over, with a belief attached to it. The last two lines name a fire by a word for crushing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The classical commentators report several named individuals as the occasion, wealthy Meccans known for mockery, and the accounts do not agree on which is meant. What they agree on is the type: a man with money enough to be untouchable, using it to make other people small. The surah gives the type rather than the name.

keyTerms.note: Two intensive forms with the same shape and rhyme, describing someone who does this habitually rather than once. Arabic uses that pattern for a trade, so the words read like job titles.
An intensive form of counting, so the money is not merely totalled but gone over again and again. It also carries the sense of setting something aside for a purpose that never arrives.
From a verb meaning to smash something to fragments, the same root as the word for a crop reduced to broken straw. Naming a fire by what it breaks rather than by what it burns is unusual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with a professional class attached to it. Poets were hired to satirise rivals, and a well-made insult could damage a clan's standing for a generation, which is why satire was feared more than a raid in some quarters. A wealthy man could buy that service. The two words opening this surah describe someone who did it himself, for pleasure.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah pairs two faults that look unrelated, mockery and hoarding, and then closes by describing a fire that reaches the hearts. The classical commentators notice the fit: the offence began in what a person thought of other people, so the punishment is described as arriving at the organ where the thought was kept.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The belief named in the third line is the surah's diagnosis: he thinks his wealth has made him last. That is not greed but a theory about death, and it explains the mockery, since a person who feels permanent can afford to be careless with others. Putting the two together makes contempt a symptom rather than a separate vice, which is a more useful account of where it comes from.

crossReferences.why: Takes the same behaviour inside a community and names each form of it separately.
Names the same accumulation and answers the same illusion about permanence with a graveyard.
Tells the same belief as a story, a wealthy man certain his holdings would outlast everything.

studies.applyIt: Notice one person you have a habit of belittling, even privately, even in a tone you would call joking. Everyone has one. For a week, say nothing about them at all, to anyone. The surah names a person by a habit rather than by an act, and a habit is only visible over several days.

studies.title: A Fire That Climbs
studies.meaning: Four short lines, each adding one thing. The fire is attributed to God by name, which happens nowhere else in the Quran; it is kindled rather than simply burning; and then it is given a verb of climbing up to see over something, the word used of the sun coming up and of a person looking over a wall. What it climbs to is the inner organ. The last two lines shut the scene: closed over them, in columns stretched out. Commentators read the columns as pillars of flame, as door bars, or as the structure of the closing itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The chapter has moved from a habit of mockery through a heap of counted money to this description, and its final third is entirely architectural. Classical sources report no occasion for the surah and note that the naming of the fire as God's own, rather than as a place or a punishment, is unique in the Book and is discussed in every major commentary.

keyTerms.note: The only place in the Quran where a fire is attached directly to God's name. The construction is read as ownership rather than as origin, which rules out any picture of a force running under its own power.

keyTerms.gloss: climbs up over, mounts to see
keyTerms.note: A verb of rising to look across something, used of the sun clearing the horizon and of a person putting his head over a wall. It gives the fire a direction and a target rather than a mere reach.
A passive participle of shutting a door and barring it. The word occurs twice in the Quran, both times of a fire closed over its occupants, and in both places in the closing lines of a short chapter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A house in Mecca was shut with a door barred from the outside, and a storeroom was closed and sealed on its contents. The word for a supporting column would have brought to mind the poles of a great tent or the pillars of the structures around the sanctuary. Both images in the final two lines are architectural, so what is described is a built enclosure rather than an open blaze on a hillside.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the fire as shut over its occupants appears in only one other place in the Quran, at the close of another very short Meccan chapter, where it also falls in the final lines. Two surahs sitting fourteen chapters apart therefore end on the identical image of a door closed from outside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the fire as God's own removes the idea of impersonal machinery grinding on by itself, which is how punishment is most often imagined. The architectural vocabulary does something else. The chapter began with a man assembling a heap of money and believing it had made him permanent; it ends by describing a structure with columns, built and closed, and the permanence he wanted is supplied in a form he did not choose.

crossReferences.why: Ends another short chapter with the same word for a fire closed over those inside it.
Shows the same failure from another angle, a man whose wealth and earnings did nothing for him.
Describes a fire whose enclosure surrounds those in it, using a different word for the same closing.

studies.applyIt: Think of a resentment you have been keeping warm for more than a year, the one you can start up again in a second. Say the person's name to yourself once, without rehearsing the story. This passage describes a fire that climbs to reach the heart, and the one you are keeping is already there.
